review:
There's a lot this remaster does well, but as of launch, there is a whole lot that needs fixing.
At least original owners got this free! If they expected us to rebuy the game in this state, this launch would have been REALLY bad.

The new lighting and texture work is overall great, no complaints about that. As for some more important things though...

Now for the issues that I've noticed that need to be fixed:
1. Cloth physics are bugged in the main game. All the physics but cloth work fine, the cloth is stuck at the lowest quality setting from the original no matter what setting you use here. It works fine in the DLCs. Probably just a bug, but please don't ignore this one and leave it unpatched, the main game looks like absolute crap without cloth physics. And don't just stop at the old medium physics setting, give us the full PhysX cloth physics from the original back. Some other issues with cloth include the physics spazzing out and making odd jutting shapes, which happened in the original but is more common now. I assume it's something to do with the cloth physics being bugged in general, so if the botched physics in this remaster are repaired to their original game state, all of this might go away.

2. Some effects like smoke can now flicker and stutter. This is a very noticeable issue that wasn't in the original game, it's distracting and needs fixing ASAP.

3.Light flicker, on streetlamps and distant buildings, was present in the original but is now more noticable, possibly because of the revamped lighting. It would be nice to get a fix, but since this was an original issue, it could be a fundamental engine problem, so I won't be mad if it's not fixed.

4. Some textures that really need high-res versions still use old textures. The biggest offender is the rock texture. Now that the mountains have been made more rocky and rocks are way closer to you up on the roads, they really need to be sharper because they're so visible. Not essential to fix, but would be appreciated.

5. The eyes. Characters look overall great, but for some odd reason they removed the moving eyes from the original cutscenes, now they blink whenever their eyes change direction, and the eyes are in a new direction when they open, we no longer see them move. Some characters don't even move their eyes, no blinking or anything, they just stare blankly ahead the whole cutscene. It really makes the characters less expressive and more robotic. The fact that they covered some of this up with blinking shows that they were aware that they somehow messed it up, and instead of fixing it they tried to hide it, and didn't even do a good job at that since half the characters simply don't look anywhere but forward now. Really disappointing intentional corner-cutting, stuff like this is why I don't respect Hangar 13 that much. Take the time to do it right, you messed up something that already worked, now fix it. As with the cloth physics, just make it like the original again, copy and paste the old animations into the remaster if you have to, I can't imagine why this would be an issue short of a dumb typo or something.

If Hangar 13 fails to fix the three most important issues that they messed up from the original: the physics, flickering smoke, and eye animations, I will not buy the Mafia 1 Remastered or the future Mafia IV if they develop it. I can let III's issues slide because that was their first game of that size. But breaking things that already worked in the original Mafia II, putting shoddy bandaids on them or ignoring them entirely instead of fixing them, and releasing the remaster knowing these things are broken, is a pretty bad look that shows just how little they care. If they don't fix all three of those issues, I'm done with them.

And I know they shipped it out to another company to remaster; but since they obviously chose someone that wasn't up to the job, received a remaster that was visibly not up to par, and released it without fixing any of the new issues anyway, they might as well have broken it themselves. 

After many of Mafia III's still-present issues and now this, Hangar 13 needs to prove to the community that they care about quality by fixing this remaster. How they treat this game with patches after launch is going to be the deciding factor in whether I buy any future game with their name attached to it. The community's good will matters more than they might think; Mafia III's sales were underwhelming because of all its issues and that can happen again. If they keep messing up, the series is either going to permanently end, or get passed off to another developer that's up to the task. In short, either do the community right for once and fix some bugs, or I and many others are out.

“The Definitive Edition”. What do you think of when you hear those words? Well, technically, you can think of pretty much anything. Just because those words mean nothing. Publishers can literally sell us anything and call it “The Definitive Edition”. And [b]Mafia[/b] is a perfect example of that. At the point I write this, there are three games in the series. All of them have “The Definitive” editions and all of those editions are absolutely different. The first [b]Mafia[/b] got the best treatment. [b]2K[/b] asked their division called [b]Hangar 13[/b] (which was already merged with [b]2K Czech[/b], creators of the original game) to create a proper remake and gave them enough money to do a good job. [b]Mafia III[/b] didn't get any treatment at all. They've just released a free update that was supposed to improve graphics (spoiler alert – it failed and almost broke the entire game) and called it a day. Now, what about [b]Mafia II[/b]?

For [b]Mafia II[/b], [b]2K[/b] hired a little (about [b]100[/b] employees) British company called [b]d3t[/b] and asked them to do a quick overhaul. So... yeah. Unlike the first [b]Mafia[/b], the “Definitive” edition of the second one is not a remake, but a quick remaster. Remember what we had in [b]Shenmue[/b] remasters? Well, it was [b]d3t[/b] who worked on them. If you've played modern versions of [b]Shenmue 1[/b] and [b]2[/b], it should give you a general idea 'bout what to expect here. Take the old game, sprinkle it with some modern technology and voilà, that would be [b]$29.99[/b] (note how price of [b]Mafia II[/b] remaster is exactly the same with the one of [b]Shenmue[/b]). At least, that was the idea.

Because while [b]Shenmue[/b] was a console title, the one that only [b]DreamCast[/b] (and [b]Xbox[/b] in the case of the sequel) owners were able to play (as long as we're not talking about emulators, of course, but that's a different story), [b]Mafia II[/b] was a multiplatform game that was already presented in [b]Steam[/b]. And obviously, asking money for such a basic overhaul would have make a lot of people angry. So, [b]2K[/b] decided to play it smart and sold the new version only for console owners. Didn't make much sense for [b]Xbox One[/b] owners who still had their [b]Xbox 360[/b] discs on them (backward compatibility, ho!~), but for those who didn't have the game yet and, of course, for [b]PlayStation 4[/b] users it sure did. So, that's how it was about selling this version, while in [b]Steam[/b]? In [b]Steam[/b] everybody who already had the original version in their libraries got the new one for free, while for the rest of us the new version just replaced the old one in the store (more about that later). So... we've got an updated version and we didn't even need to pay for it. Life's good, right?

Well... technically – yes. Yes, it is. On paper. It comes with all [b]DLC[/b]s (unlike the original version, cosmetics in the remaster will unlock with time and won't be available at the beginning of the game), the textures were replaced with those of higher resolution, there's an [b]MSAA[/b] ([b]Multisample Anti-Aliasing[/b]) support, there are improved shadows and light, new technology was used for both hair and foliage, etc. Some sounds (like sounds of shooting) were also improved. In other words, like I said, on paper it's pretty cool. Unfortunately, only on paper. Because it looks like due to limited monetization, this remaster got very limited budget. And as the result... yeah. You know how it is about those quick and cheap overhauls. Instead of fixing and improving things? They just make everything worse.

First of all – nobody cared to fix the old bugs. It's not like [b]Mafia II[/b] was the buggiest game ever made (thankfully, [b]Todd Howard[/b] wasn't involved in its development in any way), but it had a series of well-known bugs that pretty much everybody who played the game before knew very well. It was only logical (yes, you can call me [b]Mr. Spock[/b], thank you) to fix those in the remaster, but like I said, nobody here bothered. Quite the opposite, it looks like the game became more buggy now. At least, while playing the remaster, I've experienced way, [i]way[/i] more weird bugs than before. One of cutscenes with [b]Harvey Epstein[/b] is broken too and looks like a mess. The color palette was changed and looks way more cold than needed, while “retro” effect was completely removed, which makes the game to look... weird. Especially for those who remember playing the original. New hair and  foliage technologies are half-broken and come with tons of visual glitches (remember [b]Cyberpunk 2077[/b]? That's the stuff.). New light looks totally out of place and may even cause troubles. Etcetera, etcetera, etcetera.

In other words, we've got the same exact game, only worse. The “Definitive” edition of [b]Mafia II[/b] is one of those cases, when it's actually a better idea to stick with the original. Sure, the original didn't have high resolution textures optimized for [b]4K[/b], but honestly, I didn't feel bad playing it on my [b]4K[/b] TV. The remaster, on the other hand, felt way worse in many ways. There's a little “but” here in a form of the exclusive [b]DLC[/b] that adds suits and cars from the other two [b]Mafia[/b] games, though. We've got [b]Tommy[/b]'s [b]Shubert Six[/b] taxi and gangster suit to remind us about good ol' days in [b]Mafia 1[/b], while from [b]Mafia III[/b] we've got [b]Lincoln[/b]'s [b]Samson Drifter[/b] (which totally breaks the balance, by the way) and army coat. Sure, it's nothing big, but... it's there and some die hard fans may be interested in it.

All in all, though, it's still a no-no. [b]PlayStation 4[/b] owners don't have much choice, but for everybody else out there it's way, [i]way[/i] better idea to stick with the original. Which... unfortunately you can't buy in [b]Steam[/b] anymore. Well, technically you can, but to get access to it you should buy this crappy remaster first (it comes with a free copy of the original version). Because, like I said, that's what crappy remasters do. They just make  everything worse. One way or another, that's pretty much it. You already played the original game before? Just forget about this remaster. Nothing good here. Totally no reason to bother. You haven't played the original yet? Wait for a good discount and pick this one up, [i]but[/i] play the original that comes with it instead. You're on [b]Xbox One[/b]? Go buy the [b]Xbox 360[/b] version. And if you're on [b]PlayStation[/b]? Congratulations, you're screwed. Dixi.

This game is one of the best in the genre. A great story that you for sure will remember and make you believe you're in some Godfather movie. No other developer ever got close to Hangar 13's depiction of "The Family Life"

However this remaster unfortunately is probably the sloppiest work I've ever seen. When even the classic version runs better, sounds better and looks better. Hear me out, here. This "remaster" mainly added higher resolution textures. But nothing else to it. Increasing the size of the game from 7GB to 40. For no good reason at all. The textures while they do look great, looks completely out of place to the rest of the world of Empire Bay and everyone in it. During a conversation you still see NPC's to your left that is completely untouched or re-textured.

Especially noticable on the landlady in Joe's building. You will find her character everywhere, as well as the "Red Fox" call-girl that shows up pretty much everywhere. Reused assets constantly. Even though this happened in the classic, it's a bit disappointing that no thought were gone into fixing things like this.

What makes the game even worse is all the bugs. It's been out for a while now and very little has been done to eliminate things that never even existed in the Classic version at release. Misaligned cameras, assets clipping (Such as wearing your hat around your throat instead of on your head) Glitching AI that seems more interested in the wall than actually apprehending you. Especially noticable during the robbery where the Irish interrupts you. When escaping from the police, they don't even exit the stairwell to the roof before you shimmy across the billboard. I had to kill them and reload twice, before I got the prompt to shimmy across. And I had to enter the stairwell and blow away the cops that seemed more interested in inspecting their shoes and the wall instead of attempting to chase us.

Another mission where the AI's aim is so good you won't even make it to the first intersection that is about 20 yards in front of you when you start the mission. I did make to the second a few times before I gave up. Restarted the whole mission just to try to get a faster car before exiting the compound after the first meeting with the Chinese.

Everything, even the game play is completely broken in comparison to the classic version of this game while looking old, still at least look homogenous. No textures stand out too much to make it look like it doesn't belong there. Which unfortunately they do a lot here.

There is nothing definite with this version of the game. It's the most disappointing remaster I have ever come across. Not even the PhysX effects work as they should, leading you to delete the folder for clothes for them to at least use the basic ones that Hangar 13 implemented to even work. Unfortunately meaning only YOUR clothes will have some kind of physics while everyone else will look like they came from the original game released 2002. How this ever passed to release is something I will never understand. They should have made a proper remake of it just like they did with the first one. And released it afterwards. I'm happy I got the game for free, courtesy of owning the original game on Steam. At least I didn't lose any money on this. Because it sure feels like a loss. Just buy the original and play through that instead.

Another glitch I forgot to mention is the sound. The volume of the conversations aren't on par with each other. One line will play super loud while another will force you to increase the volume to even hear them speak. A lot of other conversations doesn't play at all. Subtitles ON my friends.

When I first played Mafia II, it was the original release, and it absolutely floored me. The storytelling hit hard, the cinematics were on point, and the whole presentation felt like sitting through a full Hollywood crime drama where I actually cared about everyone involved. It was stylish, emotional, polished, and honestly one of the most impressive narrative experiences of that generation. Then the Definitive Edition showed up like a long-lost cousin who says he’s here to help, but somehow steals your wallet and eats all your snacks.

For a remaster that was supposed to preserve and enhance the original, it manages to introduce issues that simply did not exist before. It is almost impressive in a chaotic, scientific way, like someone took the clean original code, shook it around like a snow globe, dumped half of it, then said, “Ship it.”

Starting in Chapter 3, during the stealth section where you infiltrate a government building to steal gas stamps, there’s a guard sitting in the lobby who apparently has supernatural powers. Every time I tried to stealth takedown this man, he pulled an alarm even as he was actively being strangled. Not after. Not before. During. As if his final act on Earth was to ruin your mission out of spite. The only real solution was to pretend he didn’t exist and move on.

Then Chapter 8 arrives, and suddenly the game decides it wants to be a slideshow. You show up at a rival gang’s meeting spot, ready to shoot the place up like a normal gangster, and the framerate drops harder than a car with bricks tied to it. It is the only part of the game that suffers this horribly, so it feels like PhysX just gave up and walked off the job.

By Chapter 10, Vito begins repeating his lines like he’s stuck in an existential loop, sometimes saying the same thing two or three times right after a cutscene. By Chapter 14, things escalate into full chaos when both Vito and Joe talk over each other during gameplay, like two actors whose microphones turned on at the same time and nobody bothered to fix it. It feels like half the dialogue triggers are firing out of sync, and no one made it back to clean them up before release.

Somewhere around Chapter 16, there is a cutscene involving Vito and another character I won’t spoil. What I will spoil is that this man’s eyes are permanently glued to the left for the entire scene. He never looks at Vito once. It is like he spotted a ghost and refused to acknowledge anything else happening around him. It completely derails the moment because you’re too busy wondering if he’s okay or if his face rig ran away.

Then there is the hat situation. If Vito wears a hat in some cutscenes, it will occasionally phase into his skull and reveal the glorious alpha hole inside, the one meant to prevent clipping. Instead, the hat clips, the head clips, and suddenly your smooth cinematic scene turns into a horror film about scalp mesh exposure. Half gangster drama, half biology lesson.

And then there is the rain. In the original game, tunnels protected you from the rain, because that is how tunnels work. In the Definitive Edition, rain now passes through concrete like it is made of sponge. You drive into a tunnel, and the rain just follows you in. The road stays wet the entire time, as if the tunnel roof is purely decorative. An immersion-breaking choice if I ever saw one.

The game still plays well, and the core story is just as strong as ever, but these issues pile up and constantly remind you that this is not the version anyone asked for. The inclusion of the Samson Drifter from Mafia III only adds to the confusion. The interior is low-resolution, clearly ported in without adjustments, and for a 1970’s muscle car, it handles like it is missing half its horsepower. It looks wrong, feels wrong, and drives worse than cars in the actual 1940s setting of the game.

So here is the honest truth: Mafia II is still fantastic, but the Definitive Edition is like watching a remastered movie where they redid the audio by recording it in a bathroom. If you really want the best experience, just play the classic version with a few graphic or texture mods. You lose nothing and avoid all the new technical issues this version brings.

That’s all from me. Hopefully this saves someone a headache, because unfortunately, the Definitive Edition just does not live up to its own name.

Mafia 2 is severely underrated. The gameplay is fairly similar to GTA but it is way better than GTA V. The police will chase you and fine you for speeding, when police see you commit a crime you're wanted until you change you clothes, if you are caught stealing a car or escaping in a car that car becomes wanted and you have to change the plates, damage to cars is permanent, and you actually can run out of gas (its not annoying though because it doesn't happen often). Okay, let me start by getting this out of the way:
Mafia II is a phenomenal game, in so many ways.. If you haven't played it already, then play it!

But, if you already have played it... Do n't expect to be blown away, as the remaster is crap.

1)  some of the licensed music was removed... which RUINS the 1950's atmosphere; half the songs we sang along to as we cruised around Empire Bay are no more.
2) Okay, MOSTLY the texture quality was increased, as was the lighting-- but I've noticed so many instances of lights flickering, decals Z-Fighting constantly (flickering between the decal and the texture beneath as the camera doesn't know which to render on top),  texture pop-in, and remember I used the word "mostly"? Well, there are still loads of textures that haven't been touched-- these look even more apparent as everything around them has been improved.
3) PhysX (Or lack thereof). The phenomenal physics of the original 2010 game aren't entirely present-- some debris effects seem to be intact, but a lot has been removed-- cloth physics seem to have been removed entirely, making Vito's coat stiff as a board. Unrealistic, and super annoying as his coat physics were one of the first things I'd praise about the original after the story xD
4) THE EYES, like wtf... Characters' eyes are completely fixed in position. This completely ruins the mannerisms of characters like Henry in particular.  They are more detailed eyes though, texture wise, and they reflect the environment quite well, if only they actually f*cking moved!
5) None of the cut content. This was a real annoyance. Many people would have hoped to see the cut content, but none of it is here. It's a shame as I'm sure that alone would've made all my points so far easy to ignore.

Again, it's a phenomenal game, but this remaster is not so good... Play the original-- I'm sure there are "graphics mods" out there if you wish for a more modern look.

Mafia II is one of my favorite games of all time. And it didn't deserve the rough treatment this "Definitive" Edition gave it. For quite a good chunk of the game, everything seemed in order. Characters enhanced, some more visual effects, maybe improved sounds? It's all very... unnecessary. But not a problem, it doesn't ruin the integrity of the main game.

... Until I got in deeper and deeper into the story chapters. Then I noticed characters' faces messed up as if it was a Garry's Mod video, cutscenes with broken segments, Vito having his hat shoved down halfway into his head as the back of his head got messed up, Vito getting up from bed quite literally, with him standing up as his legs sticked through the mattress as he "woke up". AI companions never moving from one spot to help you out, but still talking during shootouts. Scripted events like tailing missions failing because the car I went after got stuck on his own, and I was keeping my distance. Characters speaking over themselves, and repeating themselves, on the SAME conversation (even in the final encounter)... the list just goes on and on.

Issues, that I've never seen in over 10 years of playing Mafia II across different machines and consoles, happen all the time, specially crashing for no reason. Mafia II doesn't need Vito's hair going fullbright white during a cutscene with emotional impact - it just pulls you out from the experience completely. D3T, the studio responsible for this, did a very subpar job on this remaster, and it is a shame.

Don't let the title fool you, the Definitive Edition lies in the Classic Mafia II version. At least the best way to play is bundled with this mess of a "remaster", but with a way too step price tag compared to before, for a half-assed "upgrade". It runs better, looks just as good (even better in some aspects) and doesn't have these annoying issues.

Mafia II is definitely worth playing, but make sure you don't rob yourself out of an enjoyable ride with these technical issues. Play the Classic version instead.

Mafia 2: Definitive Edition is the best way to play one of the most enthralling stories of the past decade. A wonderful upgrade for a wonderful title, don’t miss it.

I came back to Mafia after many years thanks to having recently played Mafia: The Old Country. This new entry didn’t impress me much – an average title that will quickly be forgotten – but paradoxically it sparked the urge to finally finish Mafia: Definitive Edition and replay Mafia II. And I have to say, these two games together feel like one big mafia saga.

Pros:
Czech dubbing and period atmosphere – the iconic voices and authentic setting make both games a unique experience. The city feels alive, especially the opening winter chapters of Mafia II, which have an unforgettable charm.
Music – a soundtrack full of classic songs (Frank Sinatra, Dean Martin and others) perfectly underscores the action and makes you feel like you’re really living in that era.
Well-written story and characters – a gangster drama that has it all: tension, humor, tragedy, and powerful moments. The characters are memorable, and their relationships still work after all these years.
Varied missions – from ordinary driving tasks to shootouts and “big hits.” Mafia II feels dynamic and never boring.
Simulation-style driving model – cars have weight, you can feel them, and each one behaves differently. Combined with police patrols, it elevates the atmosphere even further.
Nostalgia – Mafia II strongly recalls Driver 2, which is a huge plus for long-time gamers.
Mafia II DLCs – Joe’s Adventures and Jimmy’s Vendetta add plenty of extra content beyond the main story and make up for the fact that the city otherwise serves mostly as a backdrop.

Cons:
Dated gameplay – at its core it’s now just a classic cover shooter with no real innovations.
AI and technical flaws – enemies sometimes behave stiffly, and occasional bugs can appear.
Mafia II’s ending – deliberately open and controversial. For some it’s a brilliant narrative choice, for others a frustrating cliffhanger.
Mafia: Definitive Edition on PC – initially had issues running properly, which I only managed to fix thanks to a community solution I found on a forum.
Mafia II: Definitive Edition on PC – surprisingly lacks Steam Cloud support, which feels like a big oversight for a 2020 remaster.

Verdict:
Mafia I and II remain essential experiences for anyone who loves story-driven games and gangster films. Both have preserved their unique charm – from dubbing and music to city atmosphere and dramatic twists. The gameplay may have aged, but the strength of the story and atmosphere is timeless.

For me personally, Mafia II is the highlight of the series – even after fifteen years it holds up, and its combination of winter chapters, soundtrack, nostalgia (Driver 2 vibes), and tragic storyline ranks among the best this genre has offered.

Mafia III? I gave it a chance, lasted three hours… and then uninstalled it without comment.

Score: 8/10 – classics that haven’t lost their spark even after all these years.

[h1]Intro[/h1]
[h3](Spoiler-Free Review)[/h3]
[b]Mafia II Definitive Edition[/b] (M2DE) is a remastered edition of the original Mafia II from 2010, set in Empire Bay in a timeframe spanning from 1940s to late 1950s. The game narrates the story of Vito Scaletta, an Italian immigrant which, along with his family, migrated to the USA to find a better life. The protagonist's early years are riddled with difficulties (as most immigrants faced back then), so at some point Vito starts small-time criminal activities - not knowing that this decision will change his destiny forever.

🟩 [b]The Good Side[/b]
[list]

[*][b]Can almost smell the gasoline![/b]
The atmosphere and setting of 1940s and 50s are recreated beautifully in Mafia II. Empire Bay proves to be a vibrant, beautiful city - even more so in this remastered version with its updated visuals. Immersion is solid, as citizens will react realistically: for instance, by assaulting Vito after he scratched their car. There is a decent interaction level with the environment (such as buying hot dogs from a cart, for example). Music, mannerisms and ways of speaking are coherent with the times (even Italian ones: I can tell being one myself). Those seeking immersive settings will not be disappointed.

[*][b]Fear & loathing in Empire Bay[/b]
The storyline delivers everything expected by a high-tier criminal drama: violence, betrayals, loss - but also good times, sex, booze, gambling, luxury. Mafia II successfully shows how some people are not driven to criminal life by being inherently evil, but rather by sheer necessity (as in Vito's case) - while in other instances, the opposite can be also seen. The characters are well developed, especially those closer to the protagonist, which have some extent of growth as the years go by. Definitely a solid story with characters matching its quality, that does not betray the franchise's legacy.

[*][b]Not quite over yet[/b]
Mafia II offers a good chunk of additional DLC modes, all included in the Definitive version. "Jimmy's Betrayal" and "Vendetta" both trace the story of a famed hitman that served all the biggest families - while "Joe's Adventures" is a series of missions featuring one of the most important side-characters of the main story. Depending on completion rate, there may be even 10+ hours of content in these "expansions", which is almost as much as the main game. However, don't expect great differences in terms of gameplay from any of them.
[/list]

https://steamcommunity.com/sharedfiles/filedetails/?id=2388511191

🟥 [b]The Bad Side[/b]
[list]

[*][b]What's the point, then?[/b]
This second entry in the series tries to expand gameplay by adding side activities, such as reselling stolen cars or robbing shops, in order to make extra cash to spend. Other than that, it adds a more "interactive" city framework, with gun shops, clothiers, mechanics and more each with their specific function or sales inventory. While these shops can be useful at times, the side chores can be completely overlooked: the main story will always provide more than enough cash for all the guns, ammo, upgrades and clothes one would ever wish for.

[*][b]I never asked for this...[/b]
Certain fights and situations in the main story are unfair or poorly designed. For instance, in some cases combat will start with Vito standing in the middle of a room like a target dummy - on higher difficulties, it's only up to luck if he'll make it to the closest cover in time or not. This can indeed be frustrating. The worst instance is found in a specific chapter, where an enemy can spam unlimited molotovs at the protagonist, making that one a very badly designed fight. Car chases deserve a negative mention: at times the car's frame seems to not shield Vito from bullets at all, making it very RNG dependent.
[/list]

[h1]In-Depth Breakdown[/h1]
🎮 [b]Gameplay Analysis[/b]
Gameplay is divided into Exploration, Combat, Quests and Character Management.

[b]Exploration[/b]
Is performed by car over long distances, on foot in closed spaces and vehicle-free areas. Being Mafia II a linear adventure, exploration can only be done in-between those mission phases that have no time limits (most of them). Exploring the world has not a real point, save for finding achievement-related collectibles or exotic cars to add to one's garage. In each story-related location it's possible to hand around a bit more and talk with side characters for some extra lore, find some eatery to restore HP or go to a clothing shop to get changed (which can be done to evade police identification).

[b]Combat[/b]
Plays out in a rather arcade third-person shooter fashion, with Vito being able to carry a true arsenal of weapons in his pockets - ranging from pistols to military grade rifles and even grenades. Weapon handling and damage are quite realistic especially on hard difficulty, with 2-3 shots being all it takes to kill both Vito and most enemies. Headshots are a guaranteed kill on any living thing without exceptions, as it should be. Vehicles prove to be extremely resistant to damage, unless shot in the fuel intake valve or other weakspots. Melee combat is also a thing and uses dodge, counters and heavy / light attack systems to form a simplistic but enjoyable alternative to guns - just don't bring fists to a gun fight.

[b]Quests[/b]
Are mostly related to the main story, and have good variety. Sometimes, special criteria may be in place such as stealth section where being discovered triggers a game over, undercover car chases and other unique situations depending on the case.

[b]Character Management[/b]
Is performed at shops and home. In the former, Vito is able to buy guns, ammo, clothes and upgrade cars depending on the shop type, while the latter is used to restore HP (fridge food) or change owned clothes (wardrobe). A handy garage with a cap of 10 cars is available to collect the fastest rides one can find, each customizable and moddable to some extent.

[h1]▶️Introduction[/h1]
Mafia 2 is a third person open world game with a strong emphasis on storytelling. This is the successor of Mafia 1 which was one of the best games of the early 2000s. As we all know by now Mafia 2 was a worthy successor in 2010 but how does the HD Remaster stack up? Lets take a look. Mafia 2 Definitive Edition was developed by Hangar 13 and d3t and published by [url=https://store.steampowered.com/publisher/2K]2K.[/url]

Release Date : 19th May 2020 (Mafia 2, 23rd August 2010).
Last known update: 19th May 2020.


[h1]🎮Gameplay:[/h1]

[b]Are there any changes as far as gameplay goes?[/b]

[list] [*] [b]Mission design and shooting :[/b]
If you think Mafia 2 is just another ‘’copy’’ game of Grand Theft Auto you’re totally wrong, the Mafia series really takes the time to make you familiar with controls, movement and shooting, it is a slow paced third person game that sometimes might need a little bit of tactical movement. Mafia makes great use of the run and cover system and enemies usually die within a couple of shots, now level design was great in Mafia 2 as every mission had a different meaning and different way of completing. The level design of Mafia was actually ahead of its time, sadly mechanics weren’t and the game still feels a little rusty and slow compared to Mafia 3 that does actually have the mechanics as it is a much newer game. So in short, no they did not change anything and I like that decision as it keeps the purity of the game quite high.

[*] [b]Open world potential:[/b]
Granted Mafia 2 didn’t possess a huge man in 2010 and in today’s time it is worse, still the city of Empire Bay is extremely detailed with a lot of potential, the NPC and randomly generated humans in the streets of Empire Bay feel alive, for example in the snow timeline of the game you could see random people falling due to the icy roads and this honestly adds a crazy level of detail that is even by today's standards unmatched.Now as far as special events go you basically get nothing, you cannot race your cars not can you play quicktime missions which is kind of lackluster as far as stores and what you can do with your money you get a plethora of options  like boutique stores, vehicle garages and even gun shops.

[*] [b]Weather and other little details:[/b]
Weather and nighttime are actually working real time in the game, out of nowhere it might start raining and the rain is actually noticeable while driving, that's pretty rare for an open world story game that doesn’t really focus on driving that much. After your cars break down due to multiple fatal hits you can actually go out and repair it yourself just like in the 1950s. Lastly you heal yourself by consuming food and you even get custom cutscenes for this which is a great attention to detail.

You have been warned, spoilers ahead.

Vito Scarletta is the main character and his story starts back in Sicily when his parents decided to avoid the WW2 italian drama and travel to Empire Bay, USA. The remaster does improve the visuals: sharper textures, updated lighting and slightly improved character models. The city looks cleaner and more pleasant to explore, especially indoors and during night scenes. It is not a generational leap, but it is visually more comfortable than the original version.That said, the Definitive Edition is far from perfectly polished. Technical issues and minor bugs can still occur, and animations clearly show the game’s age. Mafia II: Definitive Edition is an updated release, a HD remaster, of an already HD game that features enhanced models, textures, changes to lighting and the sound engine of the game. The game does look nicer at in motion. Some changes, like the greasy hair and the somewhat shinier eyes do look a bit strange, and I have noticed a few interesting artifacts with the Ambient Occlusion implementation, but generally, the game does look nicer. The nicer graphics don't necessarily explain the fact the download size of the game is nearly 5 times larger than the original, or the performance hit, but generally, the game does look nicer. As an owner of the original PC version of Mafia II on Steam, I received this version for free, while still keeping the old version in my library, which is a big plus (unlike Rockstar and the 'Complete' Edition of GTA IV that replaced the originals completely).

BUT, there are some issues with this re-release, starting with the first thing you see when you launch the game; the launcher is pointless. When I adjusted my settings so it would run in 1080p Borderless, when the game loaded up, it was rendering out at 480p full screen, but in a 1080p frame, so the game was in a tiny corner of my screen, and I had to navigate and change the options through the in-game options menu to get it running in the correct resolution. After getting the game to run 1080p, Borderless, Maximum settings (minus MSAA, which I ran at 4X and Vignette and Chromatic Aberration off because those effects are bad on a good day), I immediately saw they had re-done the pre-rendered cutscenes. Not just an upscaling, but they had re-done from scratch. The pre-rendered scenes look quite a bit better and might run at a higher framerate as well (which might explain the file size increase somewhat). Then the game crashed. After re-launching, Borderless Windowed Mode no longer worked, and when I tried running it through the options menu, the game threw up a load of messages about Nvidia Apex/PhysX, which is still in this version, but significantly gimped, and with no clear option to enable or disable the effects. Also, despite setting it to skip the launcher, every time I restarted, the launcher would load up first.

Once I got back onto the game, now in Fullscreen instead of Borderless, it loaded the in-game cutscene, and the audio was only going through my left ear on my headset. In-game cutscenes are mono on my setup, not pre-rendered, not actual gameplay, but the in-game scenes are. The shooty shooty bang bang part ran just fine, and audio was normal. The next in-game cutscene also ran in mono. Then the train station cutscene ran normally, then the in-game drive down the hill ran normally, and then the bar cutscene ran in mono. I was able to fix this by changing the in-game audio option to stereo and restarting the game.

Once I got to run around, I saw that the cloth physics were removed. This is disappointing, I have a Nvidia GPU so I was hoping these physics extensions would still work, considering that some PhysX particles are clearly still present, but they are not. Consequently, because some PhysX effects seem to be forced on, there may be a performance hit on AMD GPU's but I do not know for certain so take this statement with a grain of salt. Lacking the full PhysX effect experience has no impact on the actual gameplay, but it is a visual feature that is missing from the Definitive Edition that belies the idea this is the Definitive Edition for some players. Also, note that I did not run the game at an unlocked frame rate, so I can't comment on whether or not they fixed the bugs caused by running at over 100 FPS, such as the slow-motion glitch. Reading around suggests they have fixed them, but I cannot confirm that right now.

Graphically, as mentioned, the remaster is a mixed bag. Faces have benefited the most, but the eyes and hair look a little strange sometimes, appearing far shinier than they did originally. Artwork is generally of a higher resolution, pre-rendered cutscenes are completely rebuilt from scratch to use higher quality assets and run at a higher resolution and framerate. Lighting changes, such as sun effects and shadows have changed, with a stronger Ambient Occlusion process (with mixed results), higher quality shadows, including better actor self-shadowing, and a draw distance that seems to be further pushed back than it was before. The game generally looks better, although some of the artistic changes might throw you off.

Audio-wise, the soundtrack is apparently equal to what was in the base game in 2016, down 16 music tracks from the original release, some of which are on the better known side of soundtrack as well. It's far from what could be a definitive release, not quite on the same level as GTA IV, or the current state of the original Mafia if you buy it on Steam now, but that's little comfort. You are not getting the full original soundtrack experience. Apparently, some further tracks are also missing from the Joe's Adventures DLC pack, but I can't verify that myself, as I don't really want to play this version of Mafia II any further due to those technical issues. There is a mod to re-add the missing music, but you shouldn't have to mod a game to get the original intended experience. Audio mixing, by my ear, sounds a bit off in some places. Some sound effects have been replaced with higher quality assets that again I think work quite well but sound mixing seems off, even after I fixed the mono sound in some of the cutscenes, something still seemed off compared to what I was expecting to hear, as though the sound mixing in-game was wrong, with loud effects playing too quietly, something that does not occur in cutscenes, where instead it seems to lean a lot on my left speaker channel.

Overall, I can't recommend playing this version over the original. It does look nicer, but there are too many issues that make the Definitive Edition an inferior edition to the original version, which is still in your library and included in this versions purchase (or on GoG). Play the classic version instead. It doesn't look far worse (Mafia II still looks quite good) and suffers from far fewer bugs. Because this is a remastered compilation, it doesn't add anything, so you aren't missing out on any additional content unless you want to play the DLC mission packs (which aren't very good to be honest), and the original might not crash as often either.

Mafia II is a great game; the remaster is not the best way to play if you just want to play the game. The new version does not make a good game bad by any means (granted, I stopped playing before the end of hour two because I had enough of having to stop, drop out, tweak and come back to get the damn thing to work), but it is a sub-par re-release. Fortunately, unlike Rockstar, 2K aren't forcing you to use this version if you don't want to and unlike Rockstar's 'Complete Edition' mess, there are actual improvements that can be mentioned. The original release still works perfectly as long as you keep under 100 FPS on modern operating systems, it's also a HD game with a far smaller install size. There are too many drawbacks to truly call this game a definitive release. The classic release is included in this package, unlike GTA IV now, so I would recommend playing that version instead if you've never played Mafia II before.

[h1]I have significant issues with this game, particularly with its save system.[/h1]
The lack of a proper save mechanism makes it difficult to maintain progress, which can be incredibly frustrating, especially when encountering bugs or disconnections.

Additionally, the achievement design feels unnecessarily tedious, and some of the DLC missions seem like they’re designed purely to stretch out the gameplay, without adding meaningful content.

Aside from the main story — Vito’s storyline, which is somewhat decent — everything else is just flaws. [u](And there’s no cloud save, but since that didn’t actually affect me, I’ll hold off criticizing that for now.)[/u]

Although this game has many flaws, I still wanted to give it a positive review at first because of Vito’s story — until I encountered a bug that became the last straw and triggered my outburst.

I’m an [b]Achievement Hunter[/b]. I worked hard to complete all those annoying achievements in the game until there was only one left — the one that requires you to drive 1,000 miles, about 1,610 kilometers, taking over ten hours.

I drove the entire distance manually without using that well-known AFK exploit to farm mileage. So yes, I drove for more than ten hours until I had only about 25 kilometers left.

That’s right — just 25 kilometers, barely ten more minutes of driving. Like an idiot, I had been manually driving aimlessly on the highway for roughly 1,585 kilometers, wasting over ten hours of my life.

Then I found out I had been disconnected from 2K.

Okay, fine — I quit the game, thinking I’d just finish the remaining 25 kilometers once the connection was back.

But when I launched the game again, hundreds of kilometers of my progress had vanished. That meant I had to spend several more hours driving all over again.

I was genuinely devastated — and furious.

I rarely give negative reviews. Even when a game has plenty of flaws or isn’t that fun, I usually just skip reviewing it.

But unless a game really pushes me to my breaking point — yes, this one did exactly that.

This is the first negative review I’ve ever written since I started leaving reviews on Steam.

I’m not just angry about the bug itself — I’m furious at the utterly inhumane achievement design combined with such a devastating glitch that destroyed an achievement I had almost in my grasp.

And then there’s the huge pile of other flaws.

Every single thing that infuriated me kept piling up, reaching a critical point, until one moment — a trigger, a fuse — set it all off, making me finally explode and break down.

A Steam friend once asked me, [u]“Have you used any save game file from internet?”[/u]
[u]I said no — I didn't use any save file.[/u]
But now… I’ve broken my word.
Yes, I have to use them.
[h3]This negative review isn’t something I gave — it’s something the game earned all by itself.[/h3]

Mafia II is one of those rare games that feels less like a traditional open world sandbox and more like stepping into a meticulously crafted crime drama. Set in the 1940s and 50s, the game immerses you in a richly detailed world of organized crime, blending powerful storytelling, memorable characters, and a beautifully realized period setting. The highlight of Mafia II is its narrative. The relationship between Vito Scaletta and his lifelong friend Joe Barbaro stands at the heart of the experience, grounding the story with emotional weight and authenticity. The writing, dialogue, and especially the voice acting are top notch, drawing you into a world where loyalty, ambition, and betrayal define every step forward. The cinematic direction is outstanding, often feeling like you’re playing through a Hollywood gangster film. The setting of Empire Bay is another standout. While the city isn’t packed with the endless activities you might find in other open world titles, its design is purposeful. From the clothing and cars to the architecture and music, everything reflects the era with painstaking attention to detail. The soundtrack deserves special mention, weaving in iconic songs from the period that perfectly complement both quiet moments and explosive action.

Gameplay is a mix of third-person shooting, hand to hand combat(which is really enjoyable especially during some chapters), and classic car driving. The mission variety keeps things engaging, with heists, shootouts, and tense narrative driven sequences that never overstay their welcome. However, the open world itself is a point of criticism. While Empire Bay looks incredible, it’s largely static more of a backdrop for the story than a playground. Side activities are limited, and once the main campaign ends, there isn’t much reason to linger beyond appreciating the city’s atmosphere. Also to note the linearity of the mission design and occasional pacing issues cause some issues, where long drives between objectives can feel like padding. Still, these moments are softened by how authentic the experience feels every element, from snowy post war streets to smoky bars, contributes to immersion.

Despite these flaws, Mafia II remains an unforgettable experience. Its dedication to cinematic storytelling and its evocative recreation of mid 20th century America make it stand apart from more traditional open world games. If you’re looking for a powerful narrative filled with heart, betrayal, and unforgettable characters, Mafia II is a must-play. The DLC is mostly forgettable and in my opinion not worth playing.

Ok, I'll address the Definitive Edition (DE) situation straight out the gate. People need to settle down, it's not that bad. If you already owned the original, you got it for free and vise versa if you bought DE first. Even so, the only difference is that there are some 'up-resed' graphics, that's it. This is definitely not the same as Mafia 1 DE (so... maybe some false advertising in that regard). Considering all that, this is the first time I have reviewed Mafia 2, so how does it hold up?

Visuals are pretty good especially for the time it was originally released. Great sound, fantastic voice acting and a banging 50's soundtrack. Overall, the open world just oozes atmosphere, the attention to detail is magnificent. I know one of the big criticisms of DE on release was the bugs, but they must have been ironed out. All I really encountered was some rare asset drop ins and some weird cosmetic issues, but almost never.

As for the game-play in this open world, everything else is very solid too. I had a ton of fun with the gun play and driving, both hold up fantastically. Each chapter/level design is unique and interesting which latches on to the story so well that I was kept on the hook from start to finish.

The story itself though? The first game really took you on a journey with a man who was forced into the life of a mobster and dealing with the woes that came with it. But this one is about two guys who have completely embraced this life, regardless of how brutal the Mafia world can be! It was so much fun to revisit these characters and take in how much they love being a gangster, no matter what is thrown their way. Seriously, one of the best open world stories ever, let along mob stories.

Overall, Mafia II: Definitive Edition tells a story that is gripping and while it may not be largely unique in the span of Mafia lore, it’s one of the best available in video game form. I genuinely cared about Vito and the terrifying criminals that surrounded him. I grew to love their antics and laugh at their quirks, and feel sorry for the situations that they found themselves in. I think it’s a little unfair to class Mafia 2 as an open-world game, because the city does nothing but offer the setting for the story to g from point a to point b. If you’re looking for a city that is brimming with side quests and random activities, you won’t find them here. What you will find is a bittersweet, interesting period piece that looks at time that is not often explored in video games, and it’s a pretty damn memorable one at that.

There is no denying that Mafia 1 and 2 are staples in the libraries and backlogs of most gamers that appreciate a good story... I loved these two games back in the day on the Xbox and I only just now revisited both of them. 

Truthfully speaking, Mafia 2 is not as good as Mafia 1, but it is certainly a gem and a "must-play" for everyone - I highly recommend playing through the two games. With that said, I bought Mafia 1 and 2 on sale and I would NEVER buy either of the two games at full price. 30 bucks for this port that has a lot of bugs (which we will talk about) is just not acceptable. I paid 5 and I felt like that was a reasonable amount for this old port. 

Took me about 10.5 hours to finish the game on Hard difficulty, so let's talk about the good, bad and ugly. Starting with the bad and ugly, 

• Stuttering gets progressively worse throughout the chapters - started off relatively fine, but by chapter 12-15 the game stuttered an insane amount to the point where it felt semi unplayable. By then I was too invested and had to just endure the terrible performance. 

•  [b] SLIGHT SPOILER INCOMING![/b] Chapter 14 is bugged and has been for years. If you decide to rob any stores during chapter 14 or rob stores in order to get enough money for Bruno, the ending cutscene will not show up and you will have to re-do this mission (which is quite long, might I add). The simple fix is to take the $22.000 when you kill Derek and then crush cars at Bruski's. 

• Way too expensive. 30 bucks for an archaic and bad port like this is outrageous. Don't ever buy this unless it's on sale. 

• A lot of visual bugs... Faces, cars, screen blinking, etc. 

• Dialogue bugs. Repeated lines and delayed lines are common. 

• No ability to free-roam? Seriously? Why was this never implemented. Even Mafia 1 had this. 

• Cops in this game are useless - you can massacre the whole city and all it takes is to speed a little bit up and they will never catch you. Massive downgrade to the cops in Mafia 1, which I found to be brutal on Classic mode. 

All in all, you can get past the bugs and enjoy the game, none of them break the game completely and I played through the whole thing without a single crash. Let's talk about the good...

Mafia 2 is a game that executes the 1940s and 1950s theme perfectly... Everything from the cars, Empire Bay which sets the tone for a fictional take on New York brilliantly, the weapons and most importantly, the characters and overall story-telling. These are without a doubt Mafia 2's strongest points. I can't praise the story enough, it is enthralling and captivating and you become heavily invested in the characters of the game, to the point where deaths in-game are felt on a personal level. It's just one of those games where you have to play through it to see what it's all about - trust me, it's worth it.

[h2]Story[/h2]
Takes place in 1945 where protagonist Vito Scaletta returns home after serving US Army to avoid prison time for a committed robbery. With the help of his partner in crime Joe Barbaro Vito tries clearing the debt tolled upon his family of a mother & a sister by his late father from a loan shark. He then begins to make gain contacts & perform jobs that leads to his involvement in mafia. There are many interesting characters you will meet & work with for the length of its gripping story. I loved every bit of it & Vito Scaletta is a name I'll never forget. 

[h2]Gameplay[/h2]
Majority of gameplay consists of you going from point A to B and sometimes C.  This gets repetitive very quickly & sucks the strength of it's ongoing storyline. Hence driving obviously fills up majority of my play time. Driving feels decent. You can customise your car with a few options in areas of paint, body & wheels then store 'em in your garage. 

Fueling / Cleaning / Repairing cars,  buying clothes from various stores around the map, consuming food from the fridge at home & buying weapons remind you that this is an open world game. All these activities are totally optional & you can finish the game without ever knowing any of these. Some achievements are tied to specific activities which apparently is needed to be done before the accepting the final mission because you cannot roam freely after the credits roll without starting a new game.

The world is beautiful, there is a part in campaign when [spoiler]we transition to a few years later scenario where the world is changed on a large scale.[/spoiler] This moment felt very fresh & appreciative when I experienced it for the first time.

[h2]DLCs[/h2]
They do offer interesting stories & cutscenes featuring characters from the campaign but at the the cost of doing repetitive strips of generic mission more than once which is boring as hell. Just finishing a DLC mission alone is a rare achievement because it requires so much will power to go through all three of them. 

[h2]Opinion[/h2]
It looks amazing, especially with ReShade. I found no bugs, no issues with anything & it was a smooth experience till the end. Thought it is a definitive edition I would've loved some extra features addressing issues mentioned above like a fast travel option or the ability to roam freely after the final mission but I guess that's not how mafia works.
